facts: At each step, several candidate vectors (eight) are drawn from the generative head.
The targets are many vectors (one hundred) sampled from the autoencoder's Gaussian posterior for the true chunk, not a single target vector.
In the energy loss, the term comparing every model sample with every target sample is weighted by two.
In the energy loss, the term comparing every pair of different model samples is subtracted.
The distances are plain distances, not squared distances.
The loss is summed over the steps of the sequence.
Feeding the previous latent vector to the Transformer was tried and hurt performance.
The Transformer's input at each step is built from the previous chunk of K tokens, not from the previous latent vector.
A small two-layer MLP compresses the K token embeddings into a single input vector.
At inference, each predicted vector is decoded by the frozen autoencoder decoder into K tokens, which become the next step's input.
The encoder outputs the mean and standard deviation of a diagonal Gaussian, and the latent vector is sampled from it.
A KL divergence term pulls that Gaussian towards a standard normal prior.
The total loss is the reconstruction loss plus the KL term weighted by a small constant (zero point zero zero one).
The purpose is a smoother latent space, discouraging precise or large-magnitude latent values.
Some latent dimensions collapse to the standard normal prior and carry no information.
Collapsed dimensions inject noise that destabilises training of the downstream language model.
Each dimension's KL term is replaced by the larger of itself and a fixed floor, so pushing it below the floor gives no reward.
The floor is zero point five.
Dropout with a rate of fifteen percent is applied to the latent vector before the decoder.
Fifteen percent of the input tokens are masked, so the encoder must infer them from context.
Both kinds of dropout are used only while training the autoencoder, not while training or running the language model.
With these choices, four tokens map to a latent vector of one hundred and twenty eight dimensions.
For a temperature of one over an integer n, draw n samples and accept only if all n are identical; otherwise restart.
A general temperature is handled by splitting one over the temperature into an integer part and a fractional remainder.
The fractional part is handled by a Bernoulli factory procedure that simulates a coin whose success probability is the sample's probability raised to the remainder.
Failing at any stage restarts the whole process.
The whole image, as non-overlapping patches, goes through the target encoder.
The target blocks are taken from the target encoder's output, not from its input.
Four target blocks are sampled, each with a scale between fifteen and twenty percent and an aspect ratio between three quarters and one and a half.
Target blocks may overlap each other.
One context block is sampled with a scale between eighty five and one hundred percent and a square aspect ratio.
Any region of the context block that overlaps a target block is removed.
Only the remaining context patches are fed through the context encoder.
The predictor takes the context encoder's output plus one mask token per patch to be predicted.
Each mask token is one shared learnable vector with a positional embedding added.
The predictor is run once per target block.

node: Likelihood-Free Estimation of the Brier Score
facts: Computing the Brier score directly needs the full predictive distribution, which CALM cannot provide.
The sum of squared probabilities is the chance that two independent samples are identical (a collision).
That term is estimated by drawing two samples and checking whether they are equal.
The probability of the true outcome is estimated by checking whether a single sample equals it.
The estimate is: first sample equals the truth, plus second sample equals the truth, minus the two samples equal each other.
The estimator is unbiased.
Scoring only the first token of each decoded chunk would ignore the quality of the chunk's other tokens.
Brier-n treats a whole n-gram as a single outcome when checking for matches.
BrierLM is the geometric mean of the Brier-1 to Brier-4 scores.
The geometric mean is multiplied by one hundred, giving a score from zero to one hundred.
The integer n is the whole-number part of one over the temperature, and the remainder is one over the temperature minus n.
First, n samples are drawn; unless they are all identical, the process restarts.
If the remainder is zero, the agreed sample is returned.
Otherwise samples are drawn one at a time, and a sample equal to the candidate returns the candidate.
On a mismatch, a uniform random number is drawn: below the remainder divided by the step count, the whole process restarts; otherwise the step count goes up by one and drawing continues.
The head refines a noise vector through a stack of residual MLP blocks.
Each block fuses the current representation with the Transformer's hidden state through two linear layers.
Each block then applies a SwiGLU layer.
A residual connection adds each block's input to its output.
A final linear layer projects the result to the size of the output vector.
The autoencoder is context-free: each chunk is encoded independently of the rest of the sequence.
The encoder embeds the K tokens and passes each embedding through a position-wise feed-forward network.
The K hidden states are flattened and compressed by a linear layer to a single hidden-sized vector.
A second feed-forward network and a linear projection then give the latent vector.
The decoder mirrors the encoder and projects to vocabulary logits with the tied input embedding matrix.
Tokens are recovered by taking the most likely token (argmax) at each position.
The autoencoder is trained with cross-entropy summed over the K token positions.
With four tokens per chunk, a latent vector of only ten dimensions already reconstructs them with high fidelity.
It targets low temperatures of the form one over n, where drawing n identical samples rarely succeeds.
It draws one large batch of N samples, with N much larger than n, and searches it for matching groups of n.
Each distinct sample's weight is the number of ways to choose n copies from how often it appears in the batch.
The output is drawn from the candidates in proportion to those weights.
If no sample appears n times, the requirement is lowered to n minus one, then n minus two, and so on, until there is a candidate.
For each target block, the squared distance between predicted and target representations is summed over the block's patches.
These sums are averaged over the target blocks.
The predictor and the context encoder are trained by gradient-based optimisation.
The target encoder is not trained by gradients: its weights are an exponential moving average of the context encoder's.
